chapters.title: Chapter 5: Running a Clean Cap Table in India

lessons.title: Case Study: One Founder's Stake From Incorporation to Series C

children.text: Meera incorporated TiffinBox with 6,000 shares and 60% of a company worth ₹1 lakh. Eight years later she holds 5,400 shares and 11.19% of a company that has raised ₹71.07 crore and just been repriced downwards. This lesson walks the entire journey in one place, marks the four decisions that mattered most, and ends with what her stake is actually worth under two very different endings.

body.text: No single round destroyed Meera's ownership. Eight ordinary decisions, each defensible on its own day, compounded into a 60% stake becoming 11.19%. That is the normal path, and the founders who do best are simply the ones who saw each step coming.

body.title: Every event that moved the cap table

events.title: Incorporation
events.description: 10,000 shares at ₹10 face value. Meera 6,000, Rohan 4,000. Authorised capital ₹1 lakh, which will shortly become a problem.

events.title: ESOP pool and angel round
events.description: A 1,000-option pool is created, then three angels invest ₹50 lakh at ₹4,000 per share for 1,250 shares. Authorised capital is raised via Form SH-7 before the allotment. Meera falls to 48.98%.

events.title: A ₹32 lakh convertible note
events.description: Signed quickly, with a 20% discount and a ₹10 crore valuation cap. The cap table records an estimate of 500 shares. The contract will eventually say 584.

events.title: Seed round
events.description: ₹4 crore at ₹8,000 per share for 5,000 CCPS, with the pool topped up to 2,000 options. Meera falls to 31.86%.

events.title: Series A, and the pool shuffle
events.description: ₹6.25 crore at a ₹25 crore post-money. The note converts at its cap into 584 shares and the pool is reset to 15%, both pre-money. Meera falls to 21.39%, and the price per share rises only from ₹8,000 to ₹8,911.

events.title: Series B, and a secondary
events.description: ₹40 crore at a ₹200 crore post-money, at ₹57,029 per share. Meera sells 600 shares for ₹3.42 crore gross, about ₹2.99 crore after long-term capital gains tax. She holds 5,400 shares, 15.40%.

events.title: Series C, a down round
events.description: ₹20 crore at a ₹60 crore pre-money, ₹17,108 per share. Broad-based weighted average anti-dilution gives the Series B 1,488 extra shares. Meera ends at 11.19%.

body.title: Ownership across eight years (% fully diluted)

children.text: The founders' line includes Meera's secondary sale, so it steps down at the Series B by more than the round alone would explain. The pool line falls at the Series C for the opposite reason: the pool was not topped up in a down round, so its fixed 4,209 options became a smaller slice of a larger company. That is worth noticing, because it means the team's options were diluted at exactly the moment they were already underwater.
The Cap Table at the End

body.caption: What Meera actually receives, under two exits

body.text: Look at the ₹80 crore column twice. The 600 shares Meera sold at the Series B brought her ₹3.42 crore gross. The 5,400 shares she kept bring her ₹3.41 crore at that exit. One tenth of her holding, sold at the right moment, was worth as much as the other nine tenths. That is not an argument for selling everything. It is an argument for taking a little off the table when the opportunity exists, because paper value is a forecast and cash is a fact.

children.text: The Series C total: 35,071 shares before the round, plus 11,690 new shares for the ₹20 crore at ₹17,108, plus 1,488 anti-dilution shares for the Series B, gives 48,249. Meera's 5,400 ÷ 48,249 = 11.19%.

The ₹80 crore waterfall, stacked and 1x non-participating: the Series C compares ₹20 crore against a conversion value of 11,690 ÷ 48,249 × ₹80 crore = ₹19.38 crore and takes the preference. Then the Series B compares ₹40 crore against 9,102 ÷ 36,559 × ₹60 crore = ₹14.94 crore and takes the preference. The Series A and the seed fund do the same. That leaves ₹9.75 crore across 15,443 ordinary shares, so Meera receives 5,400 ÷ 15,443 × ₹9.75 crore = ₹3.41 crore and the founders together ₹5.93 crore.

At ₹300 crore every preference holder is better off converting, so proceeds follow ownership: Meera receives 5,400 ÷ 48,249 × ₹300 crore = ₹33.58 crore and the founders together ₹58.45 crore. The ₹70.25 crore preference stack has stopped mattering, which is what a good exit means in practice.
Four Decisions That Moved the Needle

columns.label: Decisions that helped
points: Founder vesting and leaver terms agreed before the first outside cheque
Negotiating broad-based weighted average anti-dilution, not a ratchet, at the Series B
Selling 10% of her holding at the Series B, which banked ₹3.42 crore
Keeping statutory records reconciled, so no round was delayed by diligence

columns.label: Decisions that cost her
points: A ₹32 lakh note with a ₹10 crore cap, which converted at an effective 45% discount
Carrying the note on the cap table as an estimate of 500 shares rather than the contractual 584
Accepting a 15% pre-money pool reset at the Series A without a bottom-up hiring plan
Raising ₹40 crore at a ₹200 crore valuation she could not grow into within two years

body.label: The single most expensive line
body.context: The ₹200 crore post-money added ₹40 crore to the preference stack and set a bar that the business missed, which produced the down round, the anti-dilution shares and a 4.21 point fall in Meera's stake at the Series C. Valuation you cannot grow into is borrowed from your own future proceeds.

body.title: Meera after the Series C
body.prompt: After the Series C, TiffinBox has 48,249 fully diluted shares and Meera holds 5,400 of them. What is her fully diluted stake, to two decimal places?
body.explanation: 5,400 ÷ 48,249 = 11.19%. Her share count fell only once in eight years, when she sold 600 shares in a secondary. Everything else that happened to her percentage happened in the denominator.

body.title: Name the number that never moved
body.textWithBlank: Across five financing rounds, the only thing that changed Meera's own ___ count was the secondary sale. Every other fall in her percentage came from the growing total.
body.explanation: This is the single most useful mental model in the course. Your numerator only changes if you buy or sell. Dilution is entirely a denominator story.

body.title: Which change would have helped most?
body.question: If Meera could change exactly one decision in the whole journey, which would most improve her position at the Series C?
options: Splitting equity with Rohan 55:45 instead of 60:40 at incorporation
Raising the Series B at a valuation she could realistically grow into, even if that meant a smaller headline
Selling 1,200 shares in the secondary instead of 600
Creating a smaller ESOP pool at the angel round
body.explanation: The Series B valuation drove everything that followed: a ₹40 crore preference ahead of her, a bar the business missed, a down round, anti-dilution shares for the Series B and a repriced company. A different founder split changes her starting point but not the path, a larger secondary is a modest gain, and a smaller early pool would have left the company unable to hire.

body.title: Your own eight years
body.scenario: You are two co-founders about to incorporate a company in Hyderabad. You have read this entire course. You have no investors yet, no employees, ₹15 lakh of savings between you and a product idea you both believe in.
body.prompt: What would you do in the first ninety days, specifically, to avoid the four decisions that cost Meera?
body.modelAnswer:
In the first ninety days:
1. Split equity with a written rationale. Score each of you on commitment, role, capital and expertise rather than arguing from feelings, round to clean numbers, and sign a founders' agreement the same week as incorporation.
2. Put founder vesting in place immediately. Four years with a one-year cliff, reverse vesting on issued shares, a call option at face value for unvested shares, and leaver definitions limited to genuine wrongdoing. Write it into the articles of association, not just a side agreement.
3. Assign your intellectual property to the company in writing, including anything either of you built before incorporation, and make sure neither of you is still bound by an old employer's contract.
4. Set authorised capital with headroom for the first two rounds and the full option pool, so you never delay a closing with a Form SH-7 process.
5. Build the cap table on day one, with both an issued and a fully diluted column, and adopt the rule that nothing is promised to anyone without both founders signing and the cap table being updated the same day.
6. Decide your convertible policy before anyone offers you money: no caps set at a valuation you expect to beat within a year, and every note modelled on the fully diluted cap table at a realistic next-round price on the day you sign it.
7. Treat the ₹15 lakh as a loan to the company, documented, rather than buying extra founder equity with it.
8. Put a compliance calendar in place with one owner, covering allotments, filings, certificates and the register of members.

The habit that matters most: re-run your dilution model before responding to any term sheet, including the pool reset and every convertible, and make sure the valuation you accept is one the business can grow into.

body.title: The founder's annual cap table ritual
steps: Rebuild the fully diluted cap table from source documents once a year, not from last year's spreadsheet.
Reconcile it against the register of members and the last annual return.
Re-model your ownership two rounds forward, including pool resets and every convertible.
Total the preference stack and calculate the exit price at which ordinary shares start getting paid.
Re-read the reserved matters list and check which thresholds you have crossed or fallen below.
Confirm vesting positions for every founder and every option holder.
Review whether any team liquidity or founder secondary is possible at the next round.
Save one dated, signed version and keep the supporting documents in a single folder.

body.title: The Whole Course in Twelve Cards

cards.definition: Your shares divided by every share that will exist once options are exercised and convertibles convert. The only percentage worth quoting.
The ceiling on what you may issue, measured at face value. Raise it before a round, not during one.
Founder shares held from day one but subject to buyback at a nominal price if you leave early.
Money raised divided by post-money valuation. Everyone existing keeps one minus that fraction.
An option pool created before the round, paid for entirely by existing shareholders.
The ceiling at which a convertible converts. It bites hardest when your next round is strong.
More than 25% of votes, enough to defeat any special resolution, including the one your next round needs.
Decisions requiring investor consent whatever your percentage. Where most founder frustration lives.
Total liquidation preferences that an exit must clear before ordinary shareholders are paid anything.
The anti-dilution formula to negotiate for, because a larger share count means a smaller adjustment.
Selling existing shares. The money reaches you personally and nobody is diluted.
The legal record of ownership. When your cap table disagrees with it, your cap table is wrong.

points: Meera went from 60.00% to 11.19% across five financings and one secondary, without a single unfair term being imposed on her.
Her share count changed exactly once, when she sold. Every other move in her percentage came from the denominator growing.
The Series A taught the pool lesson: a ₹25 crore post-money moved the price per share from ₹8,000 only to ₹8,911, because the pool reset and the note conversion sat in the pre-money count.
The Series B taught the valuation lesson: ₹200 crore added ₹40 crore to the preference stack and set a bar the business missed.
The Series C taught the anti-dilution lesson: broad-based weighted average cost 1,488 shares where a full ratchet would have cost 16,367.
At an ₹80 crore exit the 600 shares she sold are worth as much as the 5,400 she kept. At ₹300 crore the preference stack stops mattering and ownership finally decides everything.
The four habits that protect a founder: vest everything, model two rounds ahead, count every convertible at its contractual terms, and keep the statutory records reconciled.
Dilution is the price of building something larger than you could fund yourself. Pay it deliberately, never by accident.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not legal, tax or investment advice. TiffinBox Foods and everyone in this case study are fictional, and all valuations, prices, share counts, percentages and proceeds are illustrative rather than benchmarks or predictions. Share counts are rounded to whole shares, so percentages may differ slightly in the second decimal place and columns may not total exactly 100%. The exit calculations assume all options are exercised and ignore exercise proceeds, transaction costs, escrows, earn-outs and taxes. Real outcomes depend entirely on your own documents, facts and applicable law at the time. Consult a qualified lawyer, company secretary and chartered accountant before acting on anything in this course.
